title: ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED: WHAT IF THE MOST COMFORTING WORDS YOU BELIEVE ARE HIDING THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE?
paragraphs: ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED: WHAT IF THE MOST COMFORTING WORDS YOU BELIEVE ARE HIDING THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE?

Jesus promised that no one could snatch His sheep from His hand. But He also warned that not everyone who calls Him Lord will enter His Kingdom. So can salvation truly be lost, or have we misunderstood what it means to be saved? The answer may comfort the trembling believer, confront the comfortable sinner, and change how you follow Jesus forever.
There is a sentence that has helped countless Christians sleep peacefully at night.
“Once saved, always saved.”
Five words.
For some, they are a beautiful reminder that God's grace is stronger than human weakness.
For others, they have become a spiritual permission slip to live however they want, while assuming heaven is guaranteed.

And somewhere between those two realities stands a man who hasn't prayed sincerely in years, a woman who keeps falling into the same sin and wonders whether God has finally rejected her, a pastor who knows how to preach holiness while secretly feeding his own darkness, and a young believer who desperately loves Jesus but is terrified that one more failure will cost him eternity.
They have all heard the same sentence.
But they are not hearing the same message.
And that is where this conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because the most important question is not simply whether a Christian can lose salvation.
It is whether we have confused being saved by Jesus with merely having once said we believed in Jesus.
Imagine standing before Christ at the end of your life.
You remember the church services. The worship songs. The day you raised your hand. The baptism photographs. The Bible verses you shared on Facebook.
You remember telling people that you were saved.
Then you hear words that should make every human heart tremble.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” (Matthew 7:23, KJV)
Not “I knew you once.”
Not “You forgot to attend enough church services.”
“I never knew you.”
And suddenly, the question becomes terrifyingly clear.
What if someone can spend an entire lifetime believing they possess eternal life while never having truly surrendered to the One who gives it?
But before fear takes over, there is something else you must hear.
The same Jesus who spoke that warning also said:
“And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” (John 10:28, KJV)
Read that again.
They shall never perish.
Not “They might survive if they become flawless.”
Not “I will keep them until they disappoint Me.”
Jesus speaks of eternal life, divine protection, and the security of those who belong to Him.
How can both passages be true?
How can Jesus promise such extraordinary security while issuing such terrifying warnings?
The answer requires more than a slogan.
It requires opening the Scriptures without forcing them to say what we already want to believe.
And it requires something even more difficult.
The willingness to let the Word of God examine us.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not struggling with sin.
It is becoming comfortable enough with sin that we no longer feel the need to repent.
And sometimes the most painful spiritual condition is not rebellion.
It is loving Jesus sincerely while living under the constant fear that His mercy will eventually run out.
The Gospel confronts both.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul writes:
The Greek expression χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (chariti este sesōsmenoi) means, in context, “by grace you have been saved.”
The verb form translated “ye are saved” is a perfect passive participle joined with a present-tense verb. It emphasizes a saving action accomplished by God's grace with a continuing result.
This matters.
Salvation is not a medal awarded to people who finally become good enough.
It is God's gift to people who cannot rescue themselves.
You did not purchase your forgiveness with tears.
You did not earn your adoption through religious activity.
You did not persuade a reluctant Savior to love you.
Jesus went to the cross while humanity was still guilty.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were sinners.
Before we cleaned up our lives.
Before we learned the language of church.
Before we understood the full weight of our own brokenness.
Christ died for us.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), the Greek word was τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It expresses completion or accomplishment.
In John's account, Jesus had completed the work the Father gave Him to accomplish. His death was not an unfinished attempt at redemption waiting for human goodness to make it sufficient.
The cross is sufficient.
The sacrifice is sufficient.
Christ is sufficient.
But here is where a dangerous misunderstanding can enter.
The finished work of Jesus is not permission to abandon the Jesus who finished it.
Grace does not make rebellion holy.
Forgiveness does not rename darkness as light.
And eternal life is not a certificate of immunity from every warning Christ ever spoke.
Paul confronted this very distortion in Romans 6:1–2:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?”
The Greek response μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito) is an emphatic rejection.
Absolutely not.
Paul was not teaching that believers become incapable of sinning.
He was explaining that union with Christ changes our relationship to sin.
Sin may still tempt us.
Sin may still wound us.
We may still stumble terribly.
But sin is no longer supposed to be our cherished master.
There is a difference between a believer who falls and grieves, and a person who deliberately builds a home in darkness while claiming that grace makes repentance unnecessary.
And please hear this carefully.
The difference is not that one person is strong enough to save themselves.
The difference is what their relationship to Christ and sin reveals.
Consider Peter.
He walked with Jesus. Heard His teaching. Witnessed His miracles. Promised loyalty.
Then, in one of the darkest moments of his life, he denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that look.
The rooster had crowed.
The words had escaped Peter's mouth.
His courage had collapsed.
And suddenly, the man who promised he would die for Jesus realized he had denied Him to protect himself.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Perhaps you know something about those tears.
Maybe you promised God you would never return to that addiction.
Then you returned.
Maybe you said you would never betray another person's trust.
Then you did.
Maybe you stood in church with your hands raised while carrying a secret you could barely admit to yourself.
And afterward, when everything became quiet, you wondered whether God could still want you.
Peter's story matters because his failure was real.
But it was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The man who denied Christ became a witness to Christ.
Not because denial was harmless.
Not because sin didn't matter.
But because Jesus is merciful, and His restoring grace is greater than Peter's collapse.
Now consider Judas.
He also walked with Jesus.
He also heard the teaching.
He also occupied a place among the disciples.
But Scripture presents a very different trajectory of betrayal, remorse, and destruction.
Their stories should make us cautious about simplistic formulas.
External closeness to Christian things is not identical to saving faith.
And remorse, by itself, is not the same as turning to Christ for mercy.
We must not pretend to know everything about the hidden condition of another person's soul.
But we must allow these accounts to ask us an uncomfortable question.
Am I clinging to Christ, or merely clinging to the memory of a religious experience?
Jesus said in John 8:31:
“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed.”
The Greek verb μείνητε (meinēte) comes from menō, meaning to remain, abide, or continue.
Jesus describes discipleship in terms of continuing in His word.
Not visiting His truth once.
Not borrowing His name when convenient.
Remaining.
Abiding.
Continuing.
This does not mean that every genuine believer will demonstrate perfect obedience.
First John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
And First John 2:1 gives struggling Christians astonishing comfort:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
Notice both truths.
“Sin not.”
And, “If any man sin, we have an advocate.”
God's Word does not encourage sin.
But neither does it abandon the repentant sinner.
Jesus Christ is our advocate.
That means the exhausted believer who hates their sin and keeps returning to Christ is not instructed to despair.
They are called to confess, trust, repent, and continue walking with Him.
But the person who says, “I accepted Jesus years ago, so I can live in deliberate rebellion without concern,” should not mistake presumption for assurance.
That is not the freedom Paul preached.
That is a dangerous distortion of grace.
Now we must face the passage that has divided sincere Christians for generations.
Hebrews 6:4–6 speaks of people who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and then fallen away.
Hebrews 10:26–27 also gives a solemn warning concerning deliberate, persistent sin after receiving the knowledge of the truth.
These are not comfortable passages.
They were never intended to be.

Some Christians, particularly within Reformed traditions, understand these warnings as descriptions of people who experienced profound exposure to the Christian community and the Spirit's work without ever possessing genuine saving faith. Others understand the warnings as real possibilities of apostasy for those who had truly believed.
Both interpretations have serious theological histories, and neither should be dismissed through ridicule.
The Greek word παραπεσόντας (parapesontas) in Hebrews 6:6 means “having fallen away.” The word itself does not settle the entire theological debate over whether those described had been regenerate.
The context must be considered.
And the warnings must be allowed to retain their force.
We cannot responsibly erase them because they disturb our preferred doctrine.
Yet neither can we erase the promises of Christ.
John 6:39 records Jesus saying that the Father's will is that He should lose nothing of all that has been given to Him, but raise it up at the last day.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death, life, angels, powers, things present, things to come, nor any other creature can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Philippians 1:6 speaks of confidence that God, who began a good work, will carry it through to completion until the day of Jesus Christ.
Jude 24 praises the One who is able to keep believers from falling and present them faultless before His glory with exceeding joy.
These promises are not small.
They are breathtaking.
The Christian's hope rests in the faithfulness of God.
And here is an important point that often disappears during arguments about eternal security.

Christians who disagree about whether a truly regenerate person can finally fall away can still agree that salvation comes through Christ alone, that genuine faith is not an excuse for ongoing rebellion, that perseverance matters, and that God's people are called to trust His preserving grace.
The debate is real.
But the debate must never replace the Savior.
A person can win an argument about eternal security and still neglect prayer, repentance, love, holiness, and obedience.
And a person can become so consumed with fear of losing salvation that they forget the One who invited the weary to come to Him for rest.
Neither condition reflects the fullness of biblical assurance.
Consider the parable of the sower.
In Luke 8:13, Jesus describes people who receive the word with joy, believe for a while, and fall away in a time of testing.
That passage deserves serious attention.
Some understand the temporary belief as faith that never took lasting root. Others see it as evidence that a person can genuinely believe and later abandon that faith.
But whichever interpretation one holds, the warning remains.
An enthusiastic beginning is not the same thing as a life rooted in Christ.
A crowded altar does not automatically mean a transformed heart.
A baptism photograph does not prove lifelong discipleship.
A Christian biography on social media cannot substitute for knowing Jesus.
And perhaps this is the part that hurts most.
Because some of us have been living on yesterday's testimony while resisting today's conviction.
We talk about the day we accepted Christ.
But when was the last time we allowed His Word to correct us?
We remember when worship moved us to tears.
But when was the last time repentance changed our direction?
We tell people God knows our hearts.
And He does.
That is precisely why we should not use those words carelessly.
He knows the wounds nobody sees.
He knows the temptations we are fighting.
He knows when we are exhausted.
He knows when we are pretending.
He knows when we have stumbled and are desperate to return.
And He knows when we have made peace with something He calls us to surrender.
You can deceive a congregation.
You can deceive your family.
You can even deceive yourself.
But you cannot deceive the Lord who sees the heart.
That truth should sober the proud.
And comfort the sincere.
Because the same God who sees hidden sin also sees hidden repentance.
He sees the believer whispering, “Lord, help me,” after another humiliating failure.
He sees the mother praying in the kitchen when everyone else is asleep.
He sees the young man deleting something that has enslaved his mind for years.
He sees the person who finally confesses a secret they have carried for a decade.
He sees the exhausted soul who can barely form a prayer but still turns toward Jesus.
Do not confuse weakness with abandonment.
Do not confuse spiritual warfare with proof that God has rejected you.
Do not confuse a wounded conscience with a dead faith.
And do not confuse God's patience with His approval of unrepentant sin.
These distinctions matter because eternity matters.
First John 5:13 says:
“These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.”
Know.
Not merely hope that God might be merciful on a good day.
Not live in perpetual terror that one intrusive thought has destroyed your salvation.
John wrote so believers could know that they have eternal life.
Biblical assurance is possible.
But notice where the assurance is directed.
Toward those who believe in the Son of God.
The foundation is not confidence in our flawless performance.
It is confidence in Jesus Christ.
First John also describes the evidences of life in Him: confessing the true Christ, loving fellow believers, and taking God's commands seriously.
These are not payments for salvation.
They are marks of a life being transformed by grace.
And even those marks must be considered with pastoral care, because spiritual growth can be uneven, wounded, and painfully slow.
A bruised reed is not automatically a dead branch.
A struggling sheep is not automatically a wolf.
Jesus does not demand that the weakest believer pretend to be strong.
He calls us to Himself.
In John 10:27, immediately before His promise that His sheep will never perish, Jesus says:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Hear.
Known.
The Greek verb ἀκολουθοῦσίν (akolouthousin) means “they follow.”
In this context, Jesus describes His sheep as those who listen to His voice and follow Him.
The promise of security belongs to His sheep.
And the description of His sheep cannot simply be discarded.
Yet following Him does not mean earning the right to remain in His hand.
It means living in relationship with the Shepherd who gives life.
A sheep may stumble.
A sheep may wander.
A sheep may need rescue.
The Shepherd is not helpless.
And that is why the promise is so beautiful.
Our salvation is not secured by pretending we never fall.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Christ.
Still, the New Testament repeatedly calls believers to endure.
Jesus says in Matthew 24:13:
“But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.”
The Greek word ὑπομείνας (hypomeinas) speaks of enduring or persevering.
This statement occurs within Jesus' teaching about coming trials and persecution. It should not be isolated from its context or turned into a mathematical formula for earning eternal life.
But neither should we ignore its seriousness.
Christian discipleship is not merely a momentary decision.
It is a life of trusting and following Christ.
For Christians who hold to the perseverance of the saints, genuine believers continue because God preserves them.
For Christians who hold that genuine believers can ultimately turn away, the call to continue is a real warning against forfeiting faith.
The explanations differ.
The shared call remains.
Do not abandon Jesus.
Do not treat His mercy as something cheap.
Do not surrender to despair.
Remain in Him.
And now, perhaps, we can ask a better question than the one that began this article.
Instead of asking, “How far can I wander from Jesus and still be saved?”
What if we asked, “Why would I want to build my life away from the One who died to bring me home?”
Instead of asking, “How much sin can I keep without losing heaven?”
What if we asked, “Lord, what is this sin destroying in me, and how do I surrender it to You?”
Instead of asking, “Can I ever be forgiven after what I have done?”
What if we remembered the thief on the cross?
He had no opportunity to build an impressive religious résumé.
He could not spend decades demonstrating Christian maturity.
He could not repair every consequence of his past.
But he turned toward the crucified Jesus and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
There was no time to manufacture a lifetime of religious achievements.
There was a Savior.
There was mercy.
There was faith directed toward Christ.
And there was a promise.
That scene destroys the lie that salvation must be earned.
But it does not establish the lie that genuine faith makes repentance irrelevant.
The thief turned to Jesus.
He did not demand salvation while insisting that Jesus had no claim upon him.
He came with nothing to boast about.
And Christ was enough.
Maybe that is where your story meets his.
Maybe your past is not merely embarrassing.
Maybe it is devastating.
An affair.
An addiction.
A betrayal.
Years of religious hypocrisy.
A family you wounded.
A faith you neglected.
A private sin that has become a prison.
Or maybe your struggle is different.
Maybe you have spent years trying to be a perfect Christian because you are terrified that God will stop loving you if you fail.
You confess the same sin repeatedly, not because you love it, but because you cannot believe forgiveness could really be yours.
You read warning passages and see only condemnation.
You hear promises of grace and assume they are for everyone except you.
If that is you, listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to save yourself through endless anxiety.
It tells you to look to Christ.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV)
Those are not the words of a Savior eager to reject the repentant.
They are an invitation to come.
Come with your guilt.
Come with your questions.
Come with the damage you cannot undo.
Come with the habits you need His help to break.
Come with your fears.
Come with your whole truth.
But come to Jesus.
Not to a slogan.
Not to a denomination's preferred shorthand.
Not to a memory of an altar call as though the memory itself could save.
Come to the living Christ.
The One who died for sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who keeps His promises.
And please understand something else.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad because you got caught.
The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, involving a change of mind and direction. In the New Testament, it is a turning toward God that bears fruit in life.
Repentance is not the purchase price of grace.
It is the appropriate response to the God whose grace calls us out of darkness.
It may involve tears.
It may involve confession.
It may require restitution where possible.
It may mean ending a destructive relationship, seeking accountability, admitting a long-hidden truth, or asking for help with an addiction.
And sometimes it means getting up again after you have fallen, refusing to let shame convince you that returning to Jesus is pointless.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
But neither is it a peaceful agreement with sin.
It is a life of grace, faith, repentance, obedience, and ongoing transformation through the Holy Spirit.
This is why Titus 2:11–12 is so important:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.”
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace does not simply announce that the guilty can be forgiven.
It trains redeemed people to live differently.
Not perfectly by their own strength.
But genuinely, through God's work within them.
And when they fall, they do not need another crucifixion.
They need to return to the Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
Hebrews 7:25 declares that Jesus is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
What an astonishing hope.
Christ is not a dead religious founder whose teachings we must somehow honor from a distance.
He is the risen Lord.
Our intercessor.
Our advocate.
Our Savior.
And the One who began His work in us is worthy of our trust.
So, is “once saved, always saved” biblical assurance or a dangerous misunderstanding?
The answer depends on what someone means by those words.

If they mean that salvation is God's gracious work, that Jesus is a sufficient Savior, and that His people can trust His power to keep them, they are expressing convictions supported by profound biblical promises.

If they mean that a past religious decision guarantees heaven regardless of whether there was genuine faith, repentance, or any continuing relationship with Christ, they are promoting a dangerous misunderstanding.
And if someone uses the doctrine to silence every biblical warning about unbelief, apostasy, and persistent rebellion, they have gone beyond what a careful reading of Scripture permits.
Likewise, if someone uses the warning passages to convince every struggling believer that one failure has destroyed God's mercy, they have also distorted the biblical witness.
The question of whether a genuinely regenerate believer can finally apostatize remains disputed among faithful Christian traditions.
We should be honest about that.
But Scripture gives us no permission to turn that disagreement into an excuse for spiritual carelessness or endless fear.
The safest place for your soul is not inside a theological catchphrase.
It is in Jesus Christ.
Trust Him.
Listen to Him.
Follow Him.
Confess your sin.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in His truth.
And when you stumble, turn back toward the Shepherd rather than hiding from Him.
Because the heart of Christianity is not a desperate human attempt to become worthy of salvation.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and that those who belong to Him are called into a new life.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to religious performance.
Not from scandal to permanent shame.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not pretend the scandal never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not erase the need for repentance or the real consequences of our choices.
But through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the transforming power of the Holy Spirit.
A person once enslaved by sin can learn to walk in freedom.
A person consumed by guilt can receive mercy.
A person hardened by pride can become humble.
A person who has wandered can hear the Shepherd's voice and turn toward Him.
And a person who has spent years terrified of rejection can discover that biblical assurance is grounded in Christ, not in flawless human performance.
That is a Gospel worth defending.
That is a Gospel worth sharing.
And that is why I want to ask you something personal.
Not to win an argument.
Not to collect a religious-sounding comment.
But because someone reading your words may be fighting the same battle in silence.
Have you been using grace as an excuse to hide from repentance, or have you been living in fear that Jesus could never forgive you again?
You do not have to reveal private details publicly.
And if this message has confronted a spiritual compromise you know you need to surrender, you can simply write “no more hiding.”
Let the comment section become a place where people encourage one another toward Jesus, not a courtroom where wounded souls are shamed.
Somebody may read your words and realize they are not the only person struggling to come home.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
There is room to ask difficult questions here.
There is room to grow.
And there is always a reason to point one another back to Christ.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who may never be able to afford a shelf full of Christian books.
We want the new believer to find guidance.
The exhausted Christian to find encouragement.
The questioning soul to find sound teaching.
The struggling disciple to find resources that lead them back into Scripture.
And we want to continue expanding that work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money can purchase divine favor.
But gratitude, generosity, and a shared desire to make Christ known.
These are simple items, but they can serve as daily reminders of biblical truth, meaningful gifts, and practical ways to support the ongoing work.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
And no monthly payment can ever replace the blood shed at Calvary.
We do not purchase the message through our support.
That distinction is essential.
Because the very subject of this article reminds us that salvation belongs to the Lord.
Not to an institution.
Not to an impressive religious record.
To Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, I want you to imagine something one final time.
Not the terrifying scene of someone who merely assumed they knew Christ.
Imagine instead the exhausted believer who spent years fighting, falling, repenting, praying, growing, and learning to trust the Shepherd.
Someone whose faith was not always loud.
Someone whose hands sometimes trembled.
Someone who had seasons of doubt, moments of failure, and scars from battles nobody else understood.
But someone who kept turning toward Jesus.
Not because they were worthy.
Because He was worthy.
Not because they were strong enough to carry their own salvation.
Because Christ was mighty to save.
Not because their story was spotless.
Because the blood of Jesus cleanses from sin.
And imagine discovering that every genuine act of repentance, every quiet prayer, every return to God's Word, every step of obedience, and every moment of dependence upon His grace was never wasted.
The Lord knew.
The Lord saw.
The Lord was faithful.
This is not a promise that we can read the final judgment of every individual heart.
That belongs to God.
But it is a reason for every believer to stop treating Jesus as though He were either an indifferent Savior who excuses rebellion or an impatient Savior looking for an excuse to reject the broken.
He is neither.
He is holy.
He is merciful.
He is faithful.
And He is Lord.
So don't leave this article merely asking whether you can lose your salvation.
Ask whether you truly know the Savior.
And if you realize that you have been hiding behind a religious label, do not harden your heart.
Turn to Him today.
If you have been crushed by fear, do not run away from His promises.
Come to Him today.
If you are trapped in sin, do not call your chains freedom.
Bring them to Him today.
If you are tired of pretending, stop pretending.
You can pray right where you are:

“Lord Jesus, I need You. I confess that I have sinned against You. Forgive me for the ways I have trusted religious appearances more than Your truth, and for the times I have treated Your grace carelessly. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust Your promises without ignoring Your warnings. Give me a repentant heart, strengthen my faith, and help me follow You. I cannot save myself. My hope is in You alone. Amen.”
And when you finish praying, don't make the prayer itself your savior.
Look to Jesus.
Open His Word.
Seek fellowship with faithful believers.
Receive biblical teaching.
Pursue repentance and obedience through the strength God provides.
And keep looking to the cross.
Because in the end, the most beautiful assurance is not that you once spoke the right words.
It is that Jesus Christ is the Savior to whom you are called to entrust your life.
The greatest tragedy would be to spend your life defending the words “once saved, always saved” while never truly coming to know the Savior those words were supposed to honor.
